title: Central, Provincial and Town Responsibilities
imageAlt: A simplified teaching guide for Central, Provincial and Town Responsibilities. It distinguishes roles, actions and source limits, not identical arrangements in every colonial year.
content:
A decision from a central office needed people working in particular places. Provincial and town responsibilities connected colonial institutions with communities. A diagram can help identify these levels, but it cannot prove that every order was carried out.

The NCCA overview describes provincial posts such as alcalde mayor and corregidor. These were offices within colonial administration, not labels for every person living in a province. Arrangements varied over time and across jurisdictions. This introduction does not assign one unchanged chart to every colonial year.

Use a fictional message exercise. A central office issues instructions, a provincial official receives them, and a town record reports an action. Identify the level of each record before asking what happened to people. Do not treat a modern provincial governor or mayor as an exact substitute for a historical office.

The next questions concern responsibilities and evidence, not memorizing a complete list of officials.
clues: Different levels
Central, provincial and town institutions had different responsibilities and relationships.
Provincial posts
Alcalde mayor and corregidor were among colonial provincial administrative titles. Their use varied by jurisdiction and period.
A chart has limits
A relationship diagram does not prove delivery, enforcement or consent everywhere.
task: Which explanation uses government levels carefully?
Identify the office, place and period rather than assume one unchanged chart
Every provincial title names all residents
A chart proves every order worked
A colonial office is identical to every modern position
reason: Identify levels and historical settings. An organization chart alone does not establish implementation or universal agreement.
definition: The area or matters over which an authority has responsibilities.

title: A Town Office: The Gobernadorcillo
imageAlt: A simplified teaching guide for A Town Office: The Gobernadorcillo. It distinguishes roles, actions and source limits, not identical arrangements in every colonial year.
content:
The gobernadorcillo was a town-level official during Spanish colonial rule. The title is different from governor-general, the central office studied in Mission 1. Similar-looking words can refer to different responsibilities.

The San Andres municipal government's historical overview describes the gobernadorcillo as a leader of a pueblo, or town, with administrative and other duties. That local overview is a starting source, not proof of identical practice in every town for the whole colonial period. Selection rules and titles changed over time.

Try a fictional museum-label task. A caption says the gobernadorcillo governed the whole colony from the central government. Correct the level before making a larger claim. Next ask which records show the actions of that official in the town.

Do not infer every resident's approval from an officeholder's title or describe historical selection procedures as the same as modern universal elections. The lesson introduces the role; it does not reconstruct one election for every period.
clues: A town role
Gobernadorcillo identifies a town-level colonial office, not the governor-general.
Different responsibilities
A title points to an office. Records of actions are still needed to evaluate how duties were carried out.
Changing arrangements
Historical selection and duties should be checked for their period, not equated automatically with modern elections.
task: A caption confuses gobernadorcillo with governor-general. What should be corrected?
The gobernadorcillo was a town-level official, distinct from the central office
Both titles always meant the same person
The town official personally governed every island
The title proves every resident voted under modern rules
reason: Distinguish the town-level gobernadorcillo from the governor-general. Duties and selection need historical context.
definition: A town-level official in Spanish colonial administration.

title: Existing Leadership and Colonial Roles
imageAlt: A simplified teaching guide for Existing Leadership and Colonial Roles. It distinguishes roles, actions and source limits, not identical arrangements in every colonial year.
content:
Local leadership did not begin with Spanish offices. Earlier missions introduced organized communities and their leaders. Colonial rule could draw on local leaders and prominent families while changing relationships of power. Continuity means something carried on; change means something became different. Both can appear in one history.

The Library of Congress discussion describes the importance of prominent local people, or principales, alongside other participants in colonial relationships. Principal?a refers to a privileged local group in the colonial setting. It was not a name for every Indigenous person or proof that all communities followed the same political path.

Cabeza de barangay is another local office title encountered in colonial records. Do not assume its duties were identical to a present-day barangay position or to every earlier datu's role. Ask which setting and rules a record describes.

Use a fictional comparison: a family maintains local influence but holds a new colonial office. Identify continuity of influence and change of institutional relationship without saying that nothing changed or that all earlier leadership vanished.
clues: Earlier communities
Local political organization preceded colonial offices. New titles did not create all leadership.
Prominent participants
Principales were prominent local participants; the term does not include every Indigenous person.
Continuity and change
Local influence could persist while offices and relationships changed. Investigate the particular place and period.
task: Which comparison recognizes continuity and change?
Some local influence could continue while colonial offices changed its institutional setting
All earlier leadership disappeared instantly everywhere
Every Indigenous person belonged to one privileged group
No relationship changed because some leaders retained influence
reason: Earlier leadership and colonial offices must be compared, not treated as either wholly identical or entirely disconnected.
definition: Something that carries on through a period of change.

title: Between an Order and a Community
imageAlt: A simplified teaching guide for Between an Order and a Community. It distinguishes roles, actions and source limits, not identical arrangements in every colonial year.
content:
An intermediary helps connect people or institutions. Local officials could communicate demands and information between colonial authorities and communities. That position could involve responsibilities, privileges and pressure. It does not establish that an intermediary agreed with every demand or represented every resident equally.

In the National Archives town-record collection, requests involve town officials and principales. Such records show local participants using administrative processes. A request is evidence of an action, not automatically evidence that the request succeeded or that everyone supported it.

Work through a fictional case: a town record reports a demand for supplies, and another document requests a change. Identify the demand and the response separately. Do not invent the result if no later record is supplied. This is a classroom exercise, not a quotation from the archive.

Later missions examine tribute and other systems in detail. Here, follow the relationship: who communicated, who was affected, what action is recorded and what remains unknown?
clues: Connecting participants
An intermediary can carry information or demands between institutions and communities.
A recorded request
A petition or request shows an attempt to seek a decision; it does not itself establish success.
People affected
An official's action is not identical to every resident's interest or private opinion.
task: A town request seeks a change but no reply is provided. What can a report establish?
The request was made; its outcome remains to be checked
The request necessarily succeeded
Every resident had identical wishes
No local participant took any action
reason: Trace demands, requests and outcomes separately. An intermediary or request cannot stand for everyone's experience.
definition: A person or group connecting other people or institutions.

title: Whose Voice Is in the Record?
imageAlt: A simplified teaching guide for Whose Voice Is in the Record?. It distinguishes roles, actions and source limits, not identical arrangements in every colonial year.
content:
A list of officials tells us who held listed positions. It does not by itself tell us how fairly they acted or what every household experienced. A petition may preserve the voice of its writers while leaving other people's views absent.

The National Archives describes records containing requests, decrees and local administrative material. Their variety helps historians investigate actions and relationships. Each document still needs its own date, setting and purpose. Do not assume that a later record reconstructs every earlier community.

Try a fictional source check. An official reports that an instruction was carried out, but a household record describes difficulty meeting it. The accounts need not answer the same question. Ask what action each records and compare the evidence instead of discarding a voice because it differs from an official account.

A report should identify whose information survives and what further evidence is needed. Do not treat all local officeholders as either heroes or villains solely because of their title; evaluate particular actions and consequences.
clues: Identify the record
A roster, petition and account of effects answer different questions.
Ask who is missing
Writers and officeholders do not automatically represent every resident.
Evaluate actions
Check what was done and its consequences rather than infer conduct from a title alone.
task: An official roster lists a town leader. Which additional claim needs separate evidence?
That the leader acted fairly and represented every household equally
That the roster names a listed official
That an office title appears in the record
That the document can be studied as a source
reason: Identify a record's purpose and viewpoint. Titles and recorded requests alone do not establish fairness, success or universal representation.
definition: A formal request asking an authority to take an action.

title: Your Local Government Report
imageAlt: A comparison guide connects earlier leadership, colonial offices and evidence about local actions. Completing this mission does not complete Chapter 7.
content: Explain local government by connecting levels, roles and people. Distinguish the governor-general from a town-level gobernadorcillo. Introduce provincial titles in context rather than treating all positions as the same office. Compare earlier local leadership with colonial roles. Prominent families and officials were participants, but they were not every Indigenous person and did not necessarily share all residents' interests. Influence could continue while institutional relationships changed. Use this fictional report frame in your own words: At [place and time], [office or participant] took part in [recorded action]. This connects with [institution or community]. The evidence supports [specific claim], but not [unsupported conclusion]. This frame is a teaching tool, not an original historical quotation. The five-question quiz checks these distinctions. Revisit a difficult topic and use targeted practice before retrying. Passing earns the mission reward once. Complete all missions, then pass the chapter challenge to earn the chapter badge.
clues: Separate levels
An office's historical level and responsibilities matter; familiar titles are not interchangeable.
Include people
Earlier leadership, local influence and new institutions must be compared in their settings.
Keep the limit
A request, title or officeholder's account does not establish success or every resident's experience.
task: Which report best connects the investigation?
Distinguish levels and changing local roles, then examine recorded actions and their effects
Treat every colonial official as the governor-general
Assume all Indigenous people belonged to the principal?a
Use a title as proof of everyone's consent and fair outcomes
reason: Explain local institutions through historical roles, continuity and change, recorded actions and the limits of representation.
definition: Acting or speaking on behalf of others; its extent needs evidence rather than assumption.
